newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi Shura council sworn in before King Fahd.
newsitem.headline: Saudi Shura council sworn in before King Fahd.

text.p: Sixty new members of Saudi Arabia's advisory Shura council were sworn in on Monday before King Fahd, signalling the start of its second four-year session, the official Saudi Press Agency (SPA) said.

Saudi newspapers said the newly-appointed members of the oil-rich kingdom's only representative body arrived in the Red Sea port city of Jeddah on a special flight from the capital Riyadh ordered by the Saudi monarch.

They were accompanied by council president Sheikh Mohammad bin Jubair, a Sunni scholar and former justice minister, who was appointed for a second term, and 30 other members whose terms were also renewed.
The Shura, launched in December 1993 as the country's first representative body for almost 60 years, has a purely advisory function and decision-making rests with the government.
Senior princes of the Saudi royal family traditionally control the country's administration, holding many top positions at a national and regional level.

The kingdom last week raised the number of members in the all-male assembly to 90 from 60, including active and retired military officers, senior government officials, business executives, prominent tribal figures and representatives of the Shi'ite Moslem minority.
King Fahd told a cabinet meeting the move would support Saudi development and ensure an adequate number of experts advised the government on a wide range of issues.
Diplomats in the kingdom said it was difficult to gauge what impact the body's new make-up would have on the political reforms Saudi Arabia introduced more than three years ago.

The king, 75 this year, promised after the 1990-91 Gulf crisis to gradually introduce political and economic reforms aimed at modernising the system of government in the world's biggest oil producer and exporter.
The establishment of the Shura and regional assemblies in 13 provinces were seen as fledgling steps towards giving Saudis more say in running the country's affairs.
Diplomats said the council's broad membership base brought together the know-how of the country's elite while providing a good sounding board for the government.

Some said the expansion also sought to grant the minority Shi'ite population a greater say. Saudi Arabia, which enforces Islamic sharia law, is predominantly Sunni Moslem. Diplomats said there were two or three Shi'ites in the new council compared with one in the previous body.
